'''Ursula W. Goodenough''' (born March 16, 1943) is a retired Professor of [[Biology]] Emerita at [[Washington University in St. Louis]], where she researched on [[eukaryotic]] algae. She authored the textbook ''Genetics'' and the best-selling book ''[[The Sacred Depths of Nature]]'' and speaks regularly about religious naturalist orientation and [[evolution]]. She contributed to the [[NPR]] blog ''13.7: Cosmos & Culture'' from 2009 to 2011.<ref>[https://www.npr.org/people/340091473/ursula-goodenough Goodenough's Contributions to NPR]</ref>

She currently serves as president of the Religious Naturalist Association. In 2023, she was elected to the [[National Academy of Sciences]].<ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.nasonline.org/news-and-multimedia/news/2023-nas-election.html | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230502194908/http://www.nasonline.org/news-and-multimedia/news/2023-nas-election.html | url-status=dead | archive-date=May 2, 2023 | title=2023 NAS Election }}</ref>
[[File:UrsulaGere.jpg|thumb|Goodenough in Dharamsala, India, with [[Richard Gere]], [[Eric Lander]] and a Buddhist [[Bhikkhu]]]]
[[File:Ursula Goodenough with Dalai Lama, India.jpg|thumb|Goodenough in Dharamsala, India, with the Dalai Lama]]
[[File:Two cells.jpg|thumb|128x128px|Mating ''Chlamydomonas'']]

==Background and Education==
Goodenough, daughter of [[Erwin Ramsdell Goodenough]] and Evelyn Goodenough Pitcher, was born on March 16, 1943, in New York City. She earned a B.A. in [[zoology]] from [[Barnard College]] in 1963, an M.A. in zoology at [[Columbia University]] in 1965, and a Ph.D. in biology at [[Harvard University]] in 1969.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=Curriculum Vitae |url=http://religious-naturalist-association.org/Curriculum_vitae_Goodenough.pdf |access-date=February 1, 2023 |website=Washington University in St. Louis}}</ref> From 1963 to 1964, she was a [[Eugene Higgins]] Fellow at [[Columbia University]] and later became an [[National Institutes of Health|NIH]] [[Predoctoral fellow|Pre-Doctoral Fellow]] at Columbia and Harvard in 1964–1969. She was an [[Assistant professor|assistant]] and [[associate professor]] of biology at Harvard from 1971 to 1978 before moving to [[Washington University in St. Louis|Washington University]].<ref name=":0" /> She wrote three editions of a widely adopted textbook, ''Genetics''. She served as president of the [[American Society for Cell Biology]] in 1984–1985, was elected to the Cellular and Developmental Biology section of the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] in 2009,<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://global.wustl.edu/three-elected-to-american-academy-of-arts-and-sciences-in-2009/ |title=Three elected to American Academy of Arts and Sciences in 2009 |access-date=2018-10-18 |archive-date=2019-02-11 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190211060745/https://global.wustl.edu/three-elected-to-american-academy-of-arts-and-sciences-in-2009/ |url-status=dead }}</ref> was elected a Fellow of the [[American Academy of Microbiology]] in 2013<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |url=https://www.asm.org/index.php/92-news-room/press-releases/91602-eighty-seven-scientists-elected-to-the-american-academy-of-microbiology |title=Eighty-Seven Scientists Elected to the American Academy of Microbiology |access-date=2018-09-21 |archive-date=2018-09-21 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180921230328/https://www.asm.org/index.php/92-news-room/press-releases/91602-eighty-seven-scientists-elected-to-the-american-academy-of-microbiology |url-status=dead }}</ref> and was awarded a Doctor of Letters ''Honoris Causa'' by the Meadville School of Theology in 2022. Since 2013, Goodenough has been listed on the Advisory Council of the [[National Center for Science Education]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://ncse.com/about/advisory-council |title=Advisory Council |website=ncse.com |publisher=[[National Center for Science Education]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130810112828/https://ncse.com/about/advisory-council |archive-date=2013-08-10 |access-date=2018-10-30}}</ref> 

Goodenough joined the [[Institute on Religion in an Age of Science]] (IRAS) in 1989 and has served continuously on its council and as its president for four years. She has presented papers and seminars on science and religion to numerous audiences, co-chaired six IRAS conferences on Star Island, and serves on the editorial board of ''[[Zygon: Journal of Religion and Science]]''.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Ursula W. Goodenough {{!}} Journey of the Universe |url=https://www.journeyoftheuniverse.org/bios/ursula-w-goodenough |access-date=2024-08-18 |website=www.journeyoftheuniverse.org |language=en}}</ref>

==Family==
Goodenough has written that women who are balancing the demands of raising children and developing a career need to understand that they can do both. She says that realizing that a child's development is influenced by many people in their lives other than their mother has helped her achieve both her personal and professional goals.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2004-11-01 |title=ASCB Newsletter |url=https://www.ascb.org/files/0411newsletter.pdf |access-date=2024-08-08 |website=The American Society for Cell Biology}}</ref> She is the mother of five children born in 1970, 1974, 1980, 1982, and 1985, respectively, and she has 9 grandchildren.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Ursula Goodenough, PhD '69 |url=https://capecod.clubs.harvard.edu/article.html?aid=153 |access-date=2024-08-08 |website=capecod.clubs.harvard.edu |language=en}}</ref>

Goodenough's brothers are the solid-state physicist [[John B. Goodenough]] (1922–2023), who was the oldest recipient of the [[Nobel Prize]] at age 97, the anthropologist [[Ward Goodenough]] (1919–2013), and the cell biologist Daniel Goodenough (1945–2024).<ref>{{Cite news |last=McFadden |first=Robert D. |date=2023-06-26 |title=John B. Goodenough, 100, Dies; Nobel-Winning Creator of the Lithium-Ion Battery |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2023/06/26/science/john-goodenough-dead.html |access-date=2024-08-18 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=In Memoriam: Daniel Adino Goodenough (1944–2024) |url=https://www.ascb.org/member-news/in-memoriam-daniel-adino-goodenough-1944-2024/ |website=American Society for Cell Biology |publisher=American Society for Cell Biology |date=7 February 2024 |access-date=31 July 2026}}</ref>

==Teaching==
Goodenough was a [[Professor]] of [[Biology]] at [[Washington University in St. Louis|Washington University]] and taught a junior/senior-level [[cell biology]] course for many years. She was also an [[Associate professor|Associate Professor]] of [[Anatomy]] at the [[Washington University School of Medicine]] and an [[Adjunct professor|Adjunct Professor]] of [[Cell biology|Cell Biology]] at [[Mt. Sinai School of Medicine]].<ref name=":0" /> She also joined [[physicist]] [https://physics.wustl.edu/people/claude-bernard Claude Bernard] and [[Earth science|earth-scientist]] [[Michael Wysession]] for 10 years, teaching a course called The Epic of Evolution, directed at non-science majors. She has also taught graduate-level courses in microbial biology.<ref name=":0" />

==Dalai Lama==
In 2002, Goodenough was a member of a five-scientist panel invited by the [[Mind and Life Institute]] as part of an ongoing series of seminars on Western science for [[Tenzin Gyatso, the 14th Dalai Lama]], and his inner circle of monk scholars. Previous seminars explored particle physics and neuroscience. This was the Dalai Lama's first foray into cellular biology. Goodenough found him a quick study: "He's very interested in science and really wants to understand this stuff. We'd been told that he knew about DNA and proteins, but when I started, it became clear that he had very little background. Of course, one is left to wonder how many of the world's leaders understand DNA and proteins." Goodenough was joined by scientists [[Stuart Kauffman]], [[Steven Chu]], and [[Eric Lander]]. Goodenough was invited back to Dharamsala, India, to lecture again in 2003.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Ursula Goodenough |url=https://religiousnaturalism.org/ursula-goodenough/ |access-date=2024-08-08 |website=Religious Naturalism |language=en-US}}</ref>

[[File:Ursula2014.jpg|thumb|Photo of Goodenough taken in 2014]]

==Research==
Goodenough and colleagues have studied the molecular basis and [[evolution]] of life-cycle transitions in the [[Flagellum|flagellated]] green alga ''[[Chlamydomonas reinhardtii]]''. They have identified [[Gene|genes]] in the [[Mating-type locus|mating-type (MT) locus]] and genes regulated by MT that control the transition between [[vegetative growth]], [[Gamete|gametic]] differentiation, and [[zygote]] development. These include genes responsible for [[mate recognition]], [[uniparental inheritance]] of [[chloroplast DNA]], and gametic differentiation, allowing analysis of their function and [[evolution]] during [[speciation]].<ref name=":2" /> They have also purified and sequenced the alga's sexual [[Agglutination (biology)|agglutinins]] and identified the genes involved in transmitting [[chloroplast DNA]] and the [[Signaling pathway|sexual signaling pathway]] via [[Cyclic adenosine monophosphate|cAMP]].<ref name=":3" /> Their current interest is in the homeoproteins Gsm1 and Gsp1.<ref name=":2" /> In addition, they have established connections between [[thylakoid]] organization and [[photosynthetic capacity]] and researched the assembly of the [[Green algae|green alga's]] [[Cell wall|cell walls]].<ref name=":3" /> They have also elucidated structural features of [[Ciliary motility disorders|ciliary motility]] and explored the potential of forming [[lipid bodies]] for producing [[algal biodiesel]] as a [[transportation]] [[fuel]].<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |last=Biology |first=Department of |date=2018-06-28 |title=Ursula Goodenough |url=https://biology.wustl.edu/people/ursula-goodenough |access-date=2024-08-08 |website=Department of Biology |language=en}}</ref> Her research also focuses on the molecular [[Genetics|genetic]] specification of sexual [[Phenotypic trait|traits]] in pikoeukaryotic [[algae]].<ref name=":0" />

== Religious Naturalist Orientation ==
Goodenough is a prominent advocate of the religious naturalist (RN) orientation, which explores the religious potential of our science-based understanding of nature. In 1998, she wrote a widely-read book on the topic, which has been extensively revised in [http://sacreddepthsofnature.com a new 2023 edition].<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Sacred Depths of Nature {{!}} How life emerged and evolved |url=http://sacreddepthsofnature.com/ |access-date=2024-08-08 |language=en-US}}</ref> She also serves as president of the Religious Naturalist Association.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Religious Naturalist Association {{!}} |url=https://religious-naturalist-association.org/ |access-date=2024-08-08 |website=religious-naturalist-association.org}}</ref> Her recent RN presentations are listed [http://sacreddepthsofnature.com/conferences/ here].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Conferences {{!}} The Sacred Depths of Nature |url=http://sacreddepthsofnature.com/conferences/ |access-date=2024-08-08 |language=en-US}}</ref>

== Other activities ==
From 1987 to 1983, she was a member of the [[Cytology|Molecular Cytology]] Study Section and an associate editor of the ''[[Journal of Cell Biology]]''. From 1994 to 1998 and 1997 to 2000, she was an associate editor of the ''[[Cell Motility and the Cytoskeleton]]'' and ''[[Journal of Phycology]]'', respectively. In 1988, she was the coordinator of the Meeting on Cell and Molecular Biology of ''Chlamydomonas'' at the [[Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory]], and in 1990, she was the coordinator of the Regional Meeting of the [[American Society for Cell Biology]] (ASCB) in [[Chicago]]. From 1990 to 1993, she was a council member and a member of the Education Committee of the ASCB. In 1992, she became the chair of the Women in Cell Biology Committee and the president of the ASCB from 1994 to 1995. In 1993, she was the chair of the [[NSF International|NSF]] and [[NASA]] Committees, and in 1997, she was a member of the [[FASEB]] Subcommittee on Ethical Issues of Genetic Research. From 1996 to 1998, she was an adjunct member of Trends in Early Research Careers at the [[Nuclear Regulatory Commission|NRC]], and in 1996, she became the president of the [[Phi Beta Kappa]] at Washington University. In 1999, she was a Phi Beta Kappa [[Visiting scholar|Visiting Scholar]] and a board member of the Science Writers Fellowship Program at the [[Marine Biological Laboratory]]. From 2001 to 2003, she was an editor of the ''[[Eukaryotic Cell (journal)|Eukaryotic Cell]]'', and from 2003 to 2009, she was the chair of the Women in Cell Biology Committee at the ASCB. In 2002, she was the coordinator of the Meeting on Cell and Molecular Biology of ''Chlamydomonas'' in Vancouver, Canada, and in 2012, she was on the [[editorial board]] of an Algal Research Project and the Scientific Advisory Committee of the Integrated Microbial Diversity at the [[Canadian Institute for Advanced Research]].<ref name=":0" />

== Public Outreach ==
In 1992, she was a member of the Center of Advanced Study in [[Religion]] and [[Science]] (CASIRAS), and from 1992 to 1996, she was the President of [[Institute on Religion in an Age of Science|IRAS]]. In 1996, she was the [[Institute on Religion in an Age of Science|IRAS]] Conference Co-Chair on the "[[Epic of evolution|Epic of Evolution]]" and a member of the Advisory Committee at the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science|AAAS]] Program of Dialogue Between Science and Religion. In 1998, she was on the Editorial Advisory Board of the [[Zygon (journal)|Zygon: Journal of Religion and Science]], and from 2002-2006, she was the Vice President for Development at [[Institute on Religion in an Age of Science|IRAS]]. In 2006, she was the Vice President for Interdisciplinary Affairs at [[Institute on Religion in an Age of Science|IRAS]], and in 2012, she was the [[Iowa Primate Learning Sanctuary]] [[Board Member]] and [[Secretary]].<ref name=":0" /> 

== Honors ==
In 1995, Goodenough won the Founder's Day Distinguished Faculty Award from [[Washington University in St. Louis|Washington University.]]<ref>{{Cite web |last=Rooney |first=Sonya |title=Research Guides: WashU History FAQ: Washington University Distinguished Faculty Award |url=https://libguides.wustl.edu/wustl-faq/DFA |access-date=2024-07-30 |website=libguides.wustl.edu |language=en}}</ref> She also won the Faculty Teaching Awards from Washington University in 1986 and 1994. In 1999, she won the Senior Career Recognition Award from the [[American Society for Cell Biology]]. In 2005, she won the Humanist Pioneer Award from the [[American Humanist Association]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Annual Humanist Awards |url=https://americanhumanist.org/awardees/ |website=American Humanist Association |publisher=American Humanist Association |access-date=3 June 2026}}</ref> In 2009, she became a Fellow of the American Women in Science and the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]]. She also became a Fellow of the [[American Society for Microbiology|American Academy of Microbiology]] in 2013, and in 2017, she became a fellow of the American Society for Cell Biology.<ref name=":0" /> In 2022, she earned her [[Doctor of Letters]] ''[[Honoris Causa]]'' from the Meadville School of Theology, and in 2023, she became a member of the [[National Academy of Sciences]].<ref name=":3">{{Cite web |title=Ursula W. Goodenough – NAS |url=https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/ursula-w-goodenough-9n8a1h/ |access-date=2024-08-08 |website=www.nasonline.org |language=en-US}}</ref>
